newsitem.title: UK: LME copper ends at lows, others drop in its wake.
newsitem.headline: LME copper ends at lows, others drop in its wake.

text.p: Copper prices fell sharply on the London Metal Exchange (LME) on Tuesday after a hefty drop in stocks failed to underpin the market.
Other base metals fell in copper's wake, dragged down by speculative selling and bearish sentiment as well as a lack of consumer buying interest.
"Even with a solid fall in copper stocks prices fell," said an analyst. "It wasn't just copper but across the board."
Three month copper futures finished the afternoon kerb at $1,890 a tonne, down $38 from Monday's close and at the low of the day. The market peaked at $1990 late last week.
Traders said price moves were again exaggerated by thin conditions overall.
Copper stocks fell 7,825 tonnes on Tuesday, with traders attributing recent drawdowns to arbitrage deals against Shanghai and Comex copper markets.
Tight supply of scrap and Russian copper in Europe were also contributing to the falls, as was the contango spread structure.
But in the longer term some traders expected stocks to start rising steadily.
"The perception is that while stocks are falling, given time they will start building again," one said.
The bearish mood in copper soon spread to other markets, where funds and speculators liquidated long positions and adopted fresh short ones, traders said.
Consumers were sidelined in the expectation of more losses.
Aluminium eased $10 to $1,367.50 having posted a fresh 2-1/4 year low of $1,357 earlier in the day.
Stocks fell 950 tonnes, but this was not enough to reverse the metal's fortune. Technical analysts pegged next support at $1,330, with resistance likely to emerge at $1,400.
Tin followed the trend, sinking to a 16-month nadir of $5,900 before bouncing to $5,975 by the close, still $45 weaker.
Lead sunk to a seven-month low despite a fall in stocks of 1,050 tonnes, but ended $1 higher at $757.
Traders said demand from the key battery sector was still limited, and covering against shortfalls from Metaleurop's Nordenham smelter were slowing.

Nickel stocks continued to build, with a net 192 tonnes moving in on Tuesday. Prices slumped to a two-month low of $7,000 and ended close to the nadir at $7,005, down $95. A test of key support at $6,910 was expected by some charists soon.
Alloy edged back to $1,220/30 from $1,230, while zinc bucked the trend and edged up $3 to $1,019.
